lesson.title: A tenth is smaller than a fifth

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is every piece on the bar shrink, from 200 mm at 5 pieces to 100 mm at 10, when you raise the number of equal pieces the metre is cut into.
interactive.title: Cut a metre into more pieces
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
A 1 m length of cable, 1000 mm, drawn as a bar with 0 at its left end and 1000 mm at its right, cut into as many equal pieces as the slider says, every piece the same length. The first piece, at the 0 end, is picked out, with its length in millimetres written on it, or just above it when the piece is too narrow, and a label above the bar naming it as a fraction of the metre: 1/5 of the metre at 5 pieces, 1/10 of the metre at 10. Under the bar is a plot: along the bottom, the number of equal pieces from 1 to 20; up the side, the length of one piece in millimetres from 0 to 1000; a curve of dots, one dot for each whole number of pieces, with the dot for your current setting picked out. The readout gives the length of each piece.

The rule is sharing. The metre is the same 1000 mm however many pieces it is in, so each equal piece is the whole shared out among the pieces: length of each piece = 1000 ÷ pieces. At the opening setting, 5 pieces, that is 1000 ÷ 5 = 200 mm, and the label reads 1/5 of the metre because five pieces of that size make the metre. Slide to 10 and each piece is 1000 ÷ 10 = 100 mm: twice the pieces, half the length, because the same metre is now shared ten ways. At 1 the single piece is the whole 1000 mm; at 2 it is 500 mm; at 4, 250 mm; at 20, 50 mm, so narrow that only its label above the bar names it. Where the division does not come out whole, the readout is rounded to the nearest millimetre, so 3 pieces shows 333. The curve of dots falls steeply at the left and flattens to the right, never rising: going from 1 piece to 2 takes 500 mm off the piece, while going from 10 to 11 takes off only 1000 ÷ 10 − 1000 ÷ 11 = 9.1 mm, because the one new piece is small and the length it needs is gathered from ten pieces instead of one. The dots never reach 0: at any count, each piece still has a length, the metre shared that many ways.
interactive.ignores: The slider stops at 20 pieces, which could suggest there is a finest cut; a whole can be cut into any number of equal pieces, and each extra one makes the pieces smaller still, though never nothing: however many pieces there are, each has a length. The curve has a dot only at whole numbers of pieces, because the bottom number of a fraction counts whole pieces; any line joining the dots is a guide for the eye, not a claim that a metre can be in two and a half equal pieces. The pieces are drawn meeting edge to edge at exact millimetres; a real cut lands where your mark and your blade put it, not on a perfect millimetre, so a 100 mm piece is honest to the precision you can measure. Only length is shown: a tenth of a board's area or of a day's load follows the same rule, the whole shared ten ways, but looks different. The picture compares pieces of one metre with one another; it says nothing about a tenth of some other whole, which may be longer or shorter than a fifth of this one.

explain.text:
Cut one whole into more equal pieces and every piece comes out smaller. That is why a tenth of a metre is shorter than a fifth of a metre, although 10 is a bigger number than 5. Remember from the last lesson that the bottom number is a claim about size: it says how many equal pieces the whole is divided into,[^1] so a piece is a fifth when five pieces of its size make the whole.

Start with what does not change. The whole is fixed: a metre of cable is 1000 mm before you cut it and 1000 mm of pieces after, however many cuts you make. Cutting shares that length out; it never adds to it. So each equal piece is the whole shared among the pieces: **the length of one piece is the whole divided by the number of pieces, so more pieces means a smaller piece.** It is the fit test from the last lesson turned round: there you divided the whole by the piece to count how many fit; here you divide the whole by the count to find the piece. Cut the metre into five equal pieces and each is 1000 ÷ 5 = 200 mm, and five of them laid end to end give the metre back. Cut it into ten equal pieces instead and the same 1000 mm is shared ten ways, so each is 1000 ÷ 10 = 100 mm. Each of the ten has nine others to make room for inside the same metre, where each of the five had only four, and that is the whole cause: more pieces sharing one unchanged whole, so less of it for each. A fraction with 1 on top, such as 1/5 or 1/10, is one piece of the whole, and textbooks call it a [[unit fraction]]; for unit fractions of one whole this is the whole story of comparing them: the bigger the bottom number, the smaller the fraction.[^2] The same holds whenever the two tops match, because then both fractions count the same number of pieces and only the piece size differs.[^3]

The slider walks it out. You can cut the metre into any number of equal pieces you like,[^4] and at 1 piece the piece is the whole 1000 mm; at 2, 500 mm; at 4, 250 mm; at 20, 50 mm. Every step up in the count is a step down in the length, so the dot on the curve under the bar never rises as you slide to the right. The curve falls steeply at first and then flattens: going from one piece to two takes 500 mm off the piece, while going from ten pieces to eleven takes off only 9.1 mm, because the one new piece is now small and the length it needs is gathered from ten pieces instead of one. And the pieces never reach nothing: at any count you choose, each still has a length, the whole shared that many ways.

The habit that gets in the way is a natural one. With whole numbers, a bigger number is more: 10 lamps are more than 5 lamps. People who study how fractions are learned find that same habit carried over, so that 1/5 is judged bigger than 1/2 because 5 is more than 2.[^5] It is whole-number knowledge stretched to cover fractions, where it does not fit.[^6] Watch it fail on the cable. Suppose a tenth of the metre really were longer than a fifth, so longer than 200 mm. Ten tenths make the metre, so ten pieces each longer than 200 mm would lay out to more than 2000 mm: two metres of cable from one. The bottom number is not the size of the piece; it is how many pieces share the whole, and when more pieces share a whole that stands still, the only way for them all to fit is for each to be smaller. The habit is not wrong everywhere: 10 pieces of cable are indeed more pieces than 5. It is wrong about the size of each one.

Two things keep the rule honest. It compares piece sizes, so on its own it decides only when both fractions count the same number of pieces: 3/10 of the metre is three 100 mm pieces, 300 mm, longer than 1/5 at 200 mm, bigger bottom and all, because three pieces are counted against one; comparing fractions whose tops differ is a later idea. And both fractions must be of the same whole,[^7] as the last two lessons kept saying: a tenth of a 50 m drum is far longer than a fifth of a metre.

**Cutting one whole into more equal pieces makes every piece smaller, because the same whole is shared out more ways; so when two fractions of one whole count the same number of pieces, the bigger bottom number names the smaller fraction, and a tenth of a metre, 100 mm, is shorter than a fifth, 200 mm.[^2][^3]**

analogy.text: Say a 230 V supply feeds a string of matching filament lamps wired in series. You know the supply voltage shares itself out across them, equally when the lamps match: two lamps, 115 V each; five, 46 V each; ten, 23 V each. Add a lamp to the string and every lamp in it dims, because the same 230 V now has to be shared among more of them. Ten lamps are more lamps than five, and each one sees less: the same reason ten equal pieces of a metre are each shorter than five.
analogy.breaks: It is a series-only fact: wire the same lamps in parallel and each sees near enough the full 230 V however many you add, so 'more means less each' is not a general law of electricity, only of sharing out a fixed whole. And real lamps are never perfectly matched, so their shares come out a little uneven, whereas a tenth of a metre is 100 mm by definition, as exactly as the cut is made.

practice.text:
Deciding which of two fractions is smaller when they count the same number of pieces (1/5 and 1/10, or 3/8 and 3/16):
- Check both are fractions of the same whole: the same metre, the same inch, the same drum. If not, the comparison is not valid.
- Check the tops match: both count the same number of pieces. For unit fractions, the top is 1 on both.
- Then the bigger bottom number is the smaller fraction: more equal pieces in the same whole, so each piece is smaller. 1/10 is smaller than 1/5; 3/16 is smaller than 3/8.
- If the tops differ, this test does not decide. The next lessons show how to rename fractions so that it can.
- To get the actual size, divide the whole by the bottom number for one piece, then multiply by the top for the number of pieces counted.

**Rule of thumb:** bigger bottom, smaller piece, when the tops match. One equal piece is the whole divided by the bottom number. The shrinking is front-loaded: the first cut halves the piece, and past ten pieces one more piece takes off less than a tenth of the piece's length.

**Worked example:** say a drawing calls for fixings along a 2.4 m run of trunking, 2400 mm, at equal spacing, and you want to know how long each bay comes out. Four equal bays: 2400 ÷ 4 = 600 mm, each bay a quarter of the run. Six equal bays: 2400 ÷ 6 = 400 mm, each a sixth. Eight equal bays: 2400 ÷ 8 = 300 mm, each an eighth. Four, six, eight: more bays every time, and the bay gets shorter every time, because the same 2400 mm is being shared out more ways. Notice too that going from four bays to six took 200 mm off the bay, while going from six to eight took only 100 mm off, even though both steps add two bays.

**Common mistakes:**
- Reading the bigger bottom number as the bigger fraction because 10 is more than 5. With matching tops it is the other way round: a bigger bottom is more pieces in the same whole, so a smaller piece.
- Using the bigger-bottom rule when the tops differ. 3/10 of a metre is 300 mm and 1/5 is 200 mm: the bigger bottom here is the bigger fraction, because three pieces are being counted against one. Match the tops first, or wait for the renaming lesson.
- Comparing fractions of different wholes. A tenth of a 50 m drum is 5 m; a fifth of a metre is 200 mm. The bottom numbers alone tell you nothing until both fractions are of the same whole.
- Expecting each extra piece to take the same amount off. From one piece of a metre to two, each piece loses 500 mm; from ten to eleven, 9.1 mm. The early cuts do most of the shrinking.
- Expecting real pieces to come out exact. A real cut lands where your mark and your blade put it, not on a perfect millimetre, so a tenth of a metre is 100 mm to the precision you can measure, which is usually all a job needs.

interactive.html:
One metre of cable, 1000 mm, cut into equal pieces: the first piece carries its length, and the dots under the bar show that length for every count from 1 to 20.

The length of one piece is the whole divided by the number of pieces: 1000 mm shared out among them.
